source_title: Federal compliance, commercial operation, and limits on state and local UAS regulation
uas_topic: Commercial operation; federal compliance; state preemption; local authority
regulated_party: Commercial and recreational UAS operators; state and political subdivisions
regulated_activity: Operating UAS and regulating UAS at the state or local level
requirement_type: Federal-compliance requirement and limited state preemption
permit_or_approval_required: No separate general state commercial permit stated
summary: South Dakota requires drone operations to comply with applicable FAA regulations and expressly permits a business lawfully operating in the state to use a drone commercially when federally compliant. State and local governments generally may not regulate UAS equipment, registration, airspace, flight paths, or pilot qualifications. Political subdivisions may adopt operation rules consistent with federal and state law, regulate their own UAS, and enforce federal restrictions. Title 50 also disclaims intrusion on exclusive federal airspace authority, so the statute does not eliminate property, facility, or other state restrictions.

Record the applicable boundary, property owner, designated-use area, notice, and permission status in the flight packet without assuming that state preemption eliminates property-use conditions.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Preserve the mission screening and factual basis for compliance with SDCL §§ 50-15-2, 50-15-7, 50-15-10, 50-15-13, including the operating area, purpose, approvals, and any relied-upon exception. Escalate ambiguous scope, conflicting client direction, or facts that could change the regulated party or activity before flight.
notes: Local ordinance research is deferred. Section 50-15-10 preserves a narrower category of consistent local operating rules while § 50-15-7 limits listed subjects.

source_title: Airspace overflight liability and preservation of privacy and trespass torts
regulated_party: Federally compliant UAS operators and affected property owners
regulated_activity: Operating in airspace over South Dakota and using UAS in conduct alleged to invade privacy or trespass
requirement_type: Limited liability protection with express tort preservation
summary: A federally compliant UAS operation in airspace over South Dakota does not, standing alone, create liability under state or local law. That protection is narrow: the same chapter expressly preserves claims when a drone is used as an instrumentality of a privacy tort or trespass under federal or state law. The provisions therefore distinguish lawful overflight from the operator's imaging, observation, physical intrusion, landing, or other conduct. They do not create a general right to enter property, use a site, collect any desired data, or disregard the chapter's separate criminal restrictions.

Brief the crew on aborting or redirecting collection when people, residences, or unrelated activity enter the sensor footprint.

regulated_activity: Intentionally photographing, recording, or otherwise observing another person in a private place

summary: Except as authorized by law, a person may not intentionally use a drone to photograph, record, or otherwise observe another person in a private place where that person has a reasonable expectation of privacy. A violation is a Class 1 misdemeanor. The statute excepts lawful law-enforcement activity, designated emergency-management work within assigned duties, and a bona fide business or governmental operation when the covered photography, recording, or observation is unintentional or incidental. The business exception is limited to incidental collection and does not authorize intentional surveillance or negate separate restrictions on data use, property access, or landing.

source_title: Careless operation, endangerment, voyeurism, and harassment
regulated_activity: Operating carelessly or for voyeuristic or harassment purposes
summary: South Dakota makes it a Class 1 misdemeanor to intentionally or willfully operate a drone in a careless manner that endangers the life or property of another person. The same section prohibits operating a drone for voyeuristic or harassment purposes. The statutory standard addresses the purpose and manner of the flight rather than imposing a separate state flight certificate or numeric operating limit. Compliance with FAA rules does not replace this state obligation, and an otherwise commercial or professionally planned mission can still violate the provision if intentionally or willfully conducted in the prohibited manner.

source_title: Landing on another owner's property or water without consent
uas_topic: Landing; property consent; emergency exceptions; damage liability
regulated_activity: Landing a drone on real property, personal property, or qualifying waters owned by another
requirement_type: Class 1 misdemeanor prohibition, affirmative defense, and exceptions
permit_or_approval_required: Yes — landowner consent unless authorized by law or an express exception applies
summary: A person generally may not land a drone on another owner's real or personal property, or on waters overlying the owner's real property, without consent; a violation is a Class 1 misdemeanor. A forced landing or technical malfunction is an affirmative defense, but the operator remains liable for resulting damage. Chapter-wide exceptions cover landings reasonably necessary for an emergency or for maintenance support involving public or private critical infrastructure, qualifying public-safety duties, and federal government or federal-contract duties. The exceptions do not erase damage exposure or create general access permission for routine commercial work.

summary: No person may operate a drone over the grounds of a prison, correctional facility, jail, juvenile detention facility, or military facility without express authorization from the facility administrator. Effective July 1, 2026, a violation is a Class 6 felony rather than a misdemeanor. Law-enforcement officers may use mitigation techniques and countermeasures authorized under § 50-15-3.1, which permits the Department of Public Safety to adopt rules defining authorized measures and training. No final implementing rule was located in the current administrative-rule collection, so operators should not infer the available countermeasures from the statute alone.

source_title: Drone delivery of contraband to correctional facilities
regulated_party: Any person using a drone to deliver covered items
regulated_activity: Delivering contraband or controlled substances to a correctional facility
summary: Using a drone to deliver contraband or a controlled substance to a state prison or other correctional facility is a Class 6 felony in addition to the penalty for the underlying contraband or controlled-substance offense. This is a payload-delivery provision, separate from the broader prohibition on operating over covered correctional grounds without administrator authorization. It does not create an exception for a commercial operator, contractor, accidental routing decision, or federally compliant flight. Ordinary AEC payloads are not the statute's target, but the provision reinforces the need to control attached equipment and avoid covered grounds.

source_title: State aircraft registration exemption for small unmanned aircraft systems
uas_topic: Aircraft registration; small UAS; weight threshold
regulated_party: Owners or lessees of aircraft operated in South Dakota
requirement_type: Small-UAS exemption from state aircraft registration
permit_or_approval_required: No state aircraft registration for qualifying small UAS
summary: South Dakota's aircraft-registration chapter requires registration and weight-based fees for covered aircraft, but § 50-11-29 exempts an individual operating a small unmanned aircraft system. Title 50 defines a small unmanned aircraft as an unmanned aircraft weighing not more than 55 pounds, including everything onboard or attached. Accordingly, the ordinary small-UAS fleet used for AEC work is outside this state aircraft-registration scheme, although federal registration remains separate. A heavier unmanned aircraft may fall within the general state registration and fee provisions, and the text should be rechecked for uncommon or heavy-platform acquisitions.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Do not add a Virginia aircraft-registration task for the unmanned aircraft covered by this express exemption. Keep the exemption citation with the fleet compliance record while continuing to screen for mission-specific property, facility, wildlife, and client requirements.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: Do not create a state-registration purchasing gate where this record expressly exempts unmanned aircraft. Keep federal registration and asset records current, and separately check whether a mission-specific permit, property rule, weight threshold, or public-client specification still affects the selected system.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Preserve the mission screening and factual basis for compliance with SDCL §§ 50-1-1, 50-11-9, 50-11-12, 50-11-29, including the operating area, purpose, approvals, and any relied-upon exception. source_title: Use of aircraft and drones to hunt, locate, or spot wildlife
regulated_party: Any aircraft or drone operator assisting wildlife activity

requirement_type: Class 1 misdemeanor prohibition with narrow predator-or-varmint exception
permit_or_approval_required: Landowner or lessee permission is required for the narrow drone exception when the operator is not the landowner
summary: South Dakota makes it a Class 1 misdemeanor to kill or attempt to kill wildlife from an aircraft or to use an aircraft to hunt, take, concentrate, drive, rally, stir up, locate, or spot a wild bird or animal. A drone may be used to locate or spot a predator or varmint only on privately owned land, by the landowner or with the landowner's or lessee's permission, outside September through November, and in full FAA compliance. The exception does not authorize general wildlife surveys performed for hunting purposes or relax separate property and resource-agency requirements.

uas_topic: Transportation projects; contractor equipment; Part 107 responsibility

permit_or_approval_required: No separate UAS permit stated; the project contract or written agreement controls service-provider equipment exceptions
summary: SDDOT permits UAS use for department functions when it improves cost efficiency, data quality, or personnel safety. Employees may not use privately owned UAS for department business, and a UAS service provider must use company-owned UAS unless a written agreement with SDDOT provides otherwise. Consultants are directed to the Consultant Service Manual. Operations must comply with Part 107 requirements for operations, pilot certification, aircraft registration, waivers or authorizations, and airworthiness; the remote pilot in command retains final authority and responsibility for safety and compliance. Emergency deployment remains subject to FAA emergency requirements.

Define in the scope and flight plan who authorizes the mission, controls the aircraft, receives the data, and is responsible for the cited records or use restrictions.
